title: Autoscaling
subtitle: Watch a lunchtime traffic spike hit a fleet, and see why reacting late hurts and how schedules and forecasts help.
learn: How reactive, scheduled, and predictive scaling differ and when each fits
Which metrics make good scaling signals (and which mislead)
Why scaling lag exists: metric delay + boot time + warm-up
How cooldowns stop the fleet from flapping up and down
The cost of over-provisioning versus the risk of under-provisioning

steps.title: How many servers do you need?
steps.body: An online shop gets 600 requests per second most of the day. Assume each instance comfortably handles 100 req/s at 60% CPU, so 6 instances is right. But the number you need changes through the day, and nobody wants to stare at a dashboard and add servers by hand. Autoscaling is software that changes the instance count for you.
steps.idea: The right fleet size moves with traffic; autoscaling is the control loop that follows it.
steps.caption: Steady state: 6 instances, 60% CPU.

steps.title: The lunch spike arrives
steps.body: At 11:45 a promotion email lands and traffic doubles to 1,200 req/s within a minute. Six instances now face twice the traffic they were sized for. At 60% CPU they handled 600 req/s, so their ceiling at 100% is only about 1,000. CPU pins at 100%, requests queue up, and p95 latency (the time under which 95% of requests finish) jumps from 120 ms to about 1.8 seconds. Some requests start timing out.
steps.idea: Too little capacity does not degrade gently; queues build and latency explodes.
steps.caption: Demand doubles, capacity does not.

steps.title: Pick a signal to scale on
steps.body: Each instance reports numbers to a metrics store, usually averaged per minute. Good signals track load and move before users suffer: average CPU, requests per instance, or for queue workers the queue depth or age of the oldest message. Memory is often a poor signal because many runtimes hold on to heap after a spike, so it tracks load weakly. Latency is useful as an alarm, but it rises only after the damage is done.
steps.idea: Scale on a metric that rises with load and falls when capacity is added, ideally a leading one.
steps.caption: Instances publish CPU to the metrics store.

steps.title: Reactive: react to what happened
steps.body: A reactive policy compares a metric to a target. With target tracking, you say keep average CPU near 60%. The autoscaler computes desired = current × (measured ÷ target), so 6 × 100 ÷ 60 = 10, and asks the cloud API for 4 more instances. Notice the catch: CPU cannot exceed 100%, so a saturated fleet hides how overloaded it truly is. Unsaturated, the load would read about 120%, and 6 × 120 ÷ 60 = 12. The real need was 12.
steps.idea: Reactive scaling is simple and handles surprises, but it only acts after load has already arrived.
steps.caption: Autoscaler decides +4 and calls the cloud API.

steps.title: Scaling lag
steps.body: Help is not instant. Metrics are aggregated per minute, so the spike is noticed about a minute late. The scaler may wait for a couple of readings to avoid false alarms. Then the cloud must start a VM and boot your app, often 60 to 120 seconds. All that time users still see 1.8 s latency. A typical total is 3 to 5 minutes from spike to relief.
steps.idea: Scaling lag = metric delay + decision delay + boot time + warm-up; reactive scaling always pays it.
steps.caption: New instances are booting; none are serving yet.

steps.title: Warm-up and the second round
steps.body: The 4 new instances join and the load balancer sends them traffic. They start cold: empty caches, unopened database connections, code not yet optimized by the runtime. So they serve less than full speed for a minute or so. CPU settles around 72%, still above target, so the scaler adds 2 more. Once warmed, 12 instances run at 60% CPU and p95 returns to about 130 ms.
steps.idea: A new instance is not full capacity the moment it boots; give it a warm-up period before counting its metrics.
steps.caption: Fleet grows 6 to 10 to 12 and latency recovers.

steps.title: Scaling in, slowly
steps.body: At 12:30 the spike ends and traffic falls back to 600 req/s. CPU drops to 30%. The scaler does not delete half the fleet at once. A cooldown (say 5 to 10 minutes) and removing only a few instances at a time make scale-in slower than scale-out. Without that, a brief dip would remove servers just before the next wave and the fleet would flap up and down, paying boot lag every time.
steps.idea: Scale out fast, scale in slow: removing capacity wrongly is costlier than keeping it a bit longer.
steps.caption: Traffic falls; instances drain a few at a time toward 6.

steps.title: Scheduled: you know the pattern
steps.body: The spike happens every weekday at 11:45, so waiting for CPU to rise is wasteful. A scheduled action raises the minimum to 12 instances at 11:35, leaving time to boot and warm up, and a second action lowers the minimum back to 6 after the peak. The spike then meets full capacity with no lag. The cost is a few extra instance-hours, and the schedule goes stale if the pattern changes, such as a holiday or a new marketing time.
steps.idea: Scheduled scaling removes lag for predictable load, but it is only as good as your calendar.
steps.caption: Capacity is added before the spike.

steps.title: Predictive: let history forecast
steps.body: Predictive scaling trains on past load, typically days to a couple of weeks of it, to forecast the next day or so and pre-launch capacity. It suits recurring daily and weekly shapes without hand-written schedules. It cannot see a surprise, like a viral post. So teams combine the three: forecast or schedule for the known shape, reactive scaling as the safety net, and a sensible minimum and maximum.
steps.idea: Forecasts handle regular rhythms; reactive scaling covers what the forecast cannot know.
steps.caption: A forecast feeds the autoscaler ahead of time.

steps.title: Choosing a policy
steps.body: Reactive scaling follows live metrics and handles surprises but lags 3 to 5 minutes. Scheduled scaling kills lag for known events. Predictive scaling learns the rhythm. Keep a minimum so you survive the first seconds of a spike, a maximum so a bug cannot buy 500 servers, and headroom (the 60% target, not 90%) because capacity arrives late. Idle headroom is the price you pay for it: holding 6 extra instances for 1 hour costs 6 instance-hours, tiny next to minutes of 1.8 s latency during the lunch peak. You can also shorten boot lag with lean images, pre-baked machine images, or a warm pool of stopped instances.
steps.idea: Autoscaling trades a little idle cost for resilience; tune target, minimum, and lag to your traffic.
steps.caption: Three policies, one fleet.

quiz.q: Six instances are overloaded and CPU reads 100% against a 60% target. Target tracking asks for 10 instances, but 12 are needed. Why is the estimate low?
options: The cloud API caps launches at 4 instances
CPU saturates at 100%, so it hides how far demand exceeds capacity
The load balancer double counts traffic
quiz.why: A saturated metric cannot show the true overload. The scaler under-adds, measures again, and adds more in a second round.

quiz.q: Traffic jumps every weekday at 11:45 and new instances need about 4 minutes to boot and warm up. What fixes the latency spike best?
options: Lower the CPU target from 60% to 50%
A scheduled action that raises the minimum before 11:45
Scaling on memory instead of CPU
quiz.why: Reactive scaling always arrives after the spike. A predictable event is best handled by adding capacity ahead of time.

quiz.q: Why do most autoscalers scale in more slowly and cautiously than they scale out?
options: Terminated instances are billed at a premium, so removing them quickly is expensive
Cloud providers rate-limit termination calls much more strictly than launches
Idle instances cost almost nothing, so there is little reason to hurry removal
Removing capacity too early risks overload and flapping, and re-adding it pays boot lag
quiz.why: Being a little over-provisioned costs money; being under-provisioned costs availability. The asymmetry justifies a cooldown on scale-in.

quiz.q: A worker fleet processes jobs from a queue. Which scaling signal is most direct?
options: Queue depth per worker (backlog divided by worker count)
Total queue depth, ignoring worker count
p95 latency of the web tier
quiz.why: Backlog per worker measures unfinished work directly and responds to added workers. CPU can look fine while the queue grows if workers wait on I/O.

cheatsheet.def: Adds or removes instances when a live metric crosses a threshold or drifts from a target. Handles surprises but always lags.
Changes capacity at set times for known patterns, such as a daily peak. No lag, but goes stale when the pattern shifts.
Forecasts load from history and launches capacity ahead of demand. Good for recurring rhythms, blind to surprises.
Keep a metric near a value (say CPU 60%). Desired count is roughly current count × measured ÷ target, rounded up.
Delay from load change to usable capacity: metric aggregation, decision time, instance boot, and warm-up. Often 3 to 5 minutes.
Period when a new instance is not yet at full speed (cold caches, fresh connections). Ignore its metrics until it is warm, and ramp traffic to it gradually.
Minimum wait after a scaling action before another. Longer for scale-in to prevent flapping.
Minimum survives the first seconds of a spike, maximum caps cost and runaway bugs, headroom (a target well below 100%) buys time while scaling.
